question: What is DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC?
title: DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC — Front Controller Pattern
direct_answer: DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller — a single servlet that intercepts every incoming HTTP request and routes it to the correct handler (controller method). It implements the Front Controller design pattern. Spring Boot auto-configures it at URL pattern `/`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring MVC request processing pipeline and the role of the front controller pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking controllers directly handle HTTP requests — DispatcherServlet is the single entry point that orchestrates the entire request flow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the full request lifecycle: DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → Controller → ViewResolver/MessageConverter → Response, mentioning each component's responsibility

sections.title: Spring MVC's Central Request Router
sections.content: **DispatcherServlet** is the heart of Spring MVC — it's a **front controller** that acts as the single entry point for all HTTP requests in your application. Think of it like a receptionist at a corporate office: every visitor (HTTP request) comes through the front desk, and the receptionist routes them to the right department (controller). Without DispatcherServlet, Spring wouldn't know how to match incoming URLs to your @RequestMapping methods. It delegates to specialized components: **HandlerMapping** finds the right controller, **HandlerAdapter** invokes it, and **ViewResolver** or **HttpMessageConverter** handles the response. In Spring Boot, you never manually register it — the framework auto-configures DispatcherServlet at the root path `/` when `spring-boot-starter-web` is on the classpath. This servlet runs inside an embedded Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow container.

sections.title: DispatcherServlet in Action with Controller Routing
Key Points
content: **Front Controller Pattern**: DispatcherServlet is the single servlet handling all requests — no need to register individual servlets per endpoint
**Auto-Configuration**: Spring Boot registers DispatcherServlet automatically when spring-boot-starter-web is present, mapping it to URL pattern `/`
**Delegation Model**: DispatcherServlet doesn't process requests itself — it delegates to HandlerMapping (routing), HandlerAdapter (invocation), and MessageConverters (serialization)
**Request Lifecycle**: HTTP request → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → Controller → ViewResolver/MessageConverter → HTTP response
**Servlet Container**: Runs inside embedded Tomcat by default in Spring Boot — the container passes requests to DispatcherServlet
**Thread-per-Request**: Each HTTP request gets its own thread from the servlet container's thread pool
**Customization**: Override WebMvcConfigurer to customize DispatcherServlet behavior — interceptors, message converters, CORS, path matching

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller — it's the single servlet that handles every incoming HTTP request in your application. Think of it as the traffic cop for your REST API. When a request comes in, DispatcherServlet doesn't process it directly. Instead, it delegates to specialized components. First, it asks HandlerMapping to find which controller method should handle the request based on the URL and HTTP method. Then it uses HandlerAdapter to actually invoke that controller method. After the method returns, DispatcherServlet uses HttpMessageConverter to serialize the Java object into JSON for the response. In Spring Boot, you don't need to configure any of this manually — the framework auto-registers DispatcherServlet at the root path when you add spring-boot-starter-web. One common mistake freshers make is thinking controllers directly receive HTTP requests. They don't. DispatcherServlet is always the entry point. It's running inside an embedded Tomcat container, and Tomcat passes every request to this one servlet. That's why it's called a front controller — it's the single entry point that orchestrates the entire request-response cycle.

question: What is HandlerMapping in Spring MVC?
title: HandlerMapping in Spring MVC — URL to Controller Method Resolution
direct_answer: HandlerMapping is the Spring MVC component that determines which controller method should handle an incoming HTTP request based on URL path, HTTP method, headers, and parameters. RequestMappingHandlerMapping is the default implementation — it scans @RequestMapping annotations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of Spring MVC internal knowledge beyond just writing @GetMapping annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing HandlerMapping exists — thinking Spring magically routes requests without understanding the lookup mechanism
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multiple HandlerMapping beans can exist with different priorities, and Spring tries them in order until one returns a handler

sections.title: The URL-to-Controller Routing Engine
sections.content: **HandlerMapping** is the component that answers the question: "Which controller method should handle this HTTP request?" When DispatcherServlet receives a request like `GET /api/users/42`, it doesn't know which method to invoke. It asks all registered HandlerMapping beans in priority order until one returns a **HandlerExecutionChain** (the controller method plus any interceptors). The most common implementation is **RequestMappingHandlerMapping**, which scans all @Controller and @RestController beans at startup, builds an internal map of URL patterns to methods, and uses it to match incoming requests. Spring Boot auto-configures this during startup. HandlerMapping considers not just the URL path but also HTTP method (GET/POST/PUT), request headers (like Accept or Content-Type), and query parameters when deciding which method matches. This is why you can have multiple methods with the same path but different HTTP methods or header constraints.

sections.title: How HandlerMapping Matches Requests to Methods
Key Points
content: **Purpose**: HandlerMapping finds which controller method should handle an incoming request based on URL, HTTP method, headers, and parameters
**RequestMappingHandlerMapping**: Default implementation that scans @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping annotations at startup
**Priority Chain**: DispatcherServlet queries multiple HandlerMapping beans in order — first match wins
**Startup Scanning**: RequestMappingHandlerMapping builds a lookup table of all @RequestMapping methods when the application starts
**HandlerExecutionChain**: HandlerMapping returns not just the controller method but also any HandlerInterceptors that should run before/after it
**Path Variables**: HandlerMapping extracts path variables like {id} from the URL and passes them to the controller method
**Content Negotiation**: Can match based on produces and consumes attributes — e.g., only invoke a method if the client sends application/json

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: HandlerMapping is the component that figures out which controller method should handle an incoming HTTP request. When DispatcherServlet receives a request, it doesn't know where to route it. So it asks the HandlerMapping beans, "Can you handle this request?" The most common HandlerMapping is RequestMappingHandlerMapping. During application startup, it scans all your controller classes and builds an internal map of URL patterns to methods. When a request comes in, it looks up that map to find the matching method. HandlerMapping considers more than just the URL path. It also checks the HTTP method — GET versus POST — and it can match based on request headers like Content-Type or Accept. That's why you can have two methods with the same URL but different HTTP methods, and Spring knows which one to call. One thing freshers often miss is that multiple HandlerMapping beans can exist in a single application. DispatcherServlet tries them in priority order. The first one that returns a handler wins. This is useful when you're mixing annotation-based controllers with other routing strategies, though that's rare in modern Spring Boot apps. The key takeaway is HandlerMapping is the routing engine — it turns an HTTP request into a specific controller method call.

question: What happens when a Spring Boot application starts with Spring MVC?
title: Spring MVC Auto-Configuration at Startup — What Spring Boot Does
direct_answer: On startup, Spring Boot auto-configures: registers DispatcherServlet at `/`, creates RequestMappingHandlerMapping by scanning all @Controller beans, configures Jackson as the default JSON HttpMessageConverter, sets up ViewResolvers for Thymeleaf if present, and registers default exception handlers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot auto-configuration for Spring MVC and what happens behind the scenes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing why adding spring-boot-starter-web is sufficient to get a working REST API — magic is auto-configuration
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention WebMvcAutoConfiguration class and how adding @EnableWebMvc disables auto-configuration, forcing manual configuration

sections.title: Spring Boot's Auto-Configuration Magic for Web Apps
sections.content: When a Spring Boot application starts with **spring-boot-starter-web** on the classpath, the framework triggers **WebMvcAutoConfiguration** — a suite of auto-configured beans that set up a fully functional web application without any XML or Java configuration from you. The process begins with scanning for @Controller and @RestController beans, building a routing table via **RequestMappingHandlerMapping**. Spring Boot then registers **DispatcherServlet** at the root URL pattern `/` inside an embedded **Tomcat** server (or Jetty/Undertow if configured). It detects **Jackson** on the classpath and auto-configures **MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter** to handle JSON serialization. If **Thymeleaf** is present, it sets up **ThymeleafViewResolver** for server-side HTML rendering. Default exception handlers, CORS support, and static resource serving from `/static`, `/public`, `/resources` directories are all configured automatically. This is why a minimal Spring Boot REST API needs only a controller class and a main method — everything else is inferred.

sections.title: Minimal Spring Boot Web Application Startup
Key Points
content: **spring-boot-starter-web**: Single dependency that triggers all Spring MVC auto-configuration — includes Tomcat, Spring MVC, and Jackson
**WebMvcAutoConfiguration**: The @Configuration class containing all auto-configured beans for Spring MVC — DispatcherServlet, HandlerMappings, MessageConverters, ViewResolvers
**Embedded Server**: Tomcat starts on port 8080 by default, listens for HTTP requests, and forwards them to DispatcherServlet
**Component Scanning**: @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan — Spring finds all @Controller, @Service, @Repository beans
**Jackson Auto-Config**: If Jackson is on classpath, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter is registered automatically for JSON serialization
**Static Resources**: Spring Boot serves files from /static, /public, /resources, /META-INF/resources directories without configuration
**Disabling Auto-Config**: Adding @EnableWebMvc disables WebMvcAutoConfiguration — you must manually configure everything

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When a Spring Boot application starts with Spring MVC, a lot happens automatically behind the scenes. First, Spring Boot detects that spring-boot-starter-web is on the classpath. This triggers WebMvcAutoConfiguration, which is a configuration class that sets up all the Spring MVC infrastructure. An embedded Tomcat server starts up on port 8080. Spring Boot registers DispatcherServlet at the root URL pattern, so every HTTP request goes through it. Then Spring scans your application for all controller classes — anything annotated with at-Controller or at-RestController. It builds a routing table using RequestMappingHandlerMapping, which maps URL patterns to controller methods. If Jackson is present, which it is by default in spring-boot-starter-web, Spring configures MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter. This is what converts your Java objects to JSON automatically. If you've added Thymeleaf as a dependency, Spring Boot also sets up ThymeleafViewResolver for rendering HTML templates. It even configures default error handling, so you get the white-label error page for 404s and 500s without writing any code. One thing that catches freshers off guard is adding at-EnableWebMvc. That annotation disables all this auto-configuration. Suddenly you have to configure everything manually, which is almost never what you want in Spring Boot.

question: What is a HandlerInterceptor in Spring MVC?
title: HandlerInterceptor in Spring MVC — Pre and Post Processing
direct_answer: HandlerInterceptor intercepts HTTP requests at the Spring MVC layer — before and after controller method execution. Used for cross-cutting concerns: authentication checks, logging, timing, rate limiting. It's Spring MVC's equivalent of a filter but operates within the Spring context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring MVC's interceptor mechanism for cross-cutting concerns and how it differs from servlet filters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring HandlerInterceptor with Servlet Filter — both intercept requests but at different layers with different capabilities
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three methods: preHandle runs before controller, postHandle runs after controller but before response, afterCompletion runs after response is sent

sections.title: Spring MVC's Request Interception Mechanism
sections.content: **HandlerInterceptor** is Spring MVC's way of running custom logic before and after controller methods execute — think of it as middleware for your controllers. It's commonly used for **cross-cutting concerns** like authentication, logging request/response details, measuring execution time, or rate limiting. Unlike a **Servlet Filter**, which operates at the servlet container level and sees all requests (including static resources), a HandlerInterceptor runs only for requests mapped to a controller method. It has access to the Spring context, so you can inject services and beans. HandlerInterceptor defines three callback methods: **preHandle** (runs before the controller method), **postHandle** (runs after the method but before the view is rendered or JSON is serialized), and **afterCompletion** (runs after the entire request finishes, even if an exception occurred). You register interceptors by implementing **WebMvcConfigurer** and overriding `addInterceptors`.

sections.title: Custom HandlerInterceptor for Request Timing
Key Points
content: **preHandle Method**: Runs before the controller method — return false to short-circuit the request (e.g., for auth failures)
**postHandle Method**: Runs after the controller method but before the response is written — useful for adding response headers or modifying the ModelAndView
**afterCompletion Method**: Runs after the entire request finishes, even if an exception was thrown — ideal for cleanup and logging
**Spring Context Access**: HandlerInterceptor is a Spring bean — you can inject services, repositories, and configuration
**Path Patterns**: Configure which URL patterns the interceptor applies to using addPathPatterns and excludePathPatterns
**vs Servlet Filter**: Filters run at container level for all requests including static files — interceptors only run for controller-mapped requests
**Order Matters**: Multiple interceptors run in the order they're registered — use order() method to control precedence

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A HandlerInterceptor is Spring MVC's way of running custom logic before and after your controller methods execute. It's like middleware for your REST API. You'd use it for things that need to happen on every request — authentication checks, logging, measuring how long requests take, or rate limiting. HandlerInterceptor has three methods. The first is preHandle, which runs before the controller method. If you return false from preHandle, Spring short-circuits the request and never calls the controller. That's useful for auth failures. The second method is postHandle. It runs after the controller finishes but before the response is sent to the client. You can use this to add response headers or modify the view for traditional MVC apps. The third method is afterCompletion, which runs after everything is done, even if an exception was thrown. This is where you'd do cleanup or final logging. One common confusion is HandlerInterceptor versus Servlet Filter. Both intercept requests, but they work at different layers. A filter runs at the servlet container level and sees every request, including static files like CSS and images. An interceptor only runs for requests that map to a controller. Also, interceptors are Spring beans, so you can inject services into them. Filters can't easily access the Spring context.

beats.content: non-obvious: postHandle is only called if the controller method succeeded. If the method throws an exception, postHandle is skipped. afterCompletion is always called — that's the right place for guaranteed cleanup.

question: What is ViewResolver in Spring MVC?
title: ViewResolver in Spring MVC — Resolving View Names to Templates
direct_answer: ViewResolver resolves a view name string returned by a @Controller method into an actual view template. For example, InternalResourceViewResolver maps "users" to /WEB-INF/views/users.jsp. ThymeleafViewResolver maps it to templates/users.html.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how traditional @Controller view resolution works for server-side HTML rendering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking ViewResolver is used in REST APIs — it's only for @Controller methods returning view names, not @RestController returning JSON
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention ContentNegotiatingViewResolver for multiple view types, and explain that @RestController bypasses ViewResolver entirely because @ResponseBody is implicit

sections.title: Turning View Names into Rendered HTML
sections.content: **ViewResolver** is the Spring MVC component that resolves a **logical view name** (a simple string like `"users"` or `"order-details"`) returned by a @Controller method into an actual **View object** that renders HTML. This is only used for traditional **server-side rendering** applications, not REST APIs. When a controller method returns a String, Spring MVC asks the configured ViewResolver to find the corresponding template file. For example, **InternalResourceViewResolver** resolves `"users"` to `/WEB-INF/views/users.jsp`, while **ThymeleafViewResolver** resolves it to `src/main/resources/templates/users.html`. The View object then renders the HTML by combining the template with model data. Spring Boot auto-configures the appropriate ViewResolver based on template engines detected on the classpath — Thymeleaf, Freemarker, Mustache, etc. Important: **@RestController** methods bypass ViewResolver entirely because they implicitly have @ResponseBody on every method, which triggers HttpMessageConverter instead.

sections.title: ViewResolver with Thymeleaf for HTML Pages
Key Points
content: **Logical View Names**: Controller methods return simple strings like "users" — ViewResolver maps them to actual template files
**ThymeleafViewResolver**: Default for Spring Boot when Thymeleaf is present — resolves names to src/main/resources/templates/<name>.html
**InternalResourceViewResolver**: Used for JSP templates — maps view names to /WEB-INF/views/<name>.jsp
**@Controller vs @RestController**: Only @Controller uses ViewResolver — @RestController has implicit @ResponseBody and uses HttpMessageConverter
**Model Data**: Controller adds data to Model object — ViewResolver passes it to the template engine for rendering
**Auto-Configuration**: Spring Boot detects template engines on classpath and configures the appropriate ViewResolver automatically
**ContentNegotiatingViewResolver**: Can return different view types (HTML, JSON, XML) based on Accept header — useful for hybrid apps

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: ViewResolver is the component that turns a view name string into an actual HTML template. This only applies to traditional Spring MVC applications that return server-rendered HTML pages, not REST APIs. When a controller method returns a string like "users", Spring MVC doesn't know what file to render. So it asks the ViewResolver to resolve that name into a View object. For example, if you're using Thymeleaf, the ThymeleafViewResolver takes "users" and resolves it to templates/users.html. If you're using JSP, InternalResourceViewResolver resolves it to WEB-INF/views/users.jsp. The View object then combines the template with the data you added to the Model and produces the final HTML. Spring Boot auto-configures the right ViewResolver based on what template engine you have on the classpath. If you add Thymeleaf, you get ThymeleafViewResolver. If you add Freemarker, you get FreemarkerViewResolver. One critical thing freshers miss is that ViewResolver is never used in REST APIs. If your controller is annotated with at-RestController, every method implicitly has at-ResponseBody. That means Spring bypasses ViewResolver and uses HttpMessageConverter instead to serialize your return value to JSON. Only at-Controller methods that return strings use ViewResolver. If you're building a REST API, you can completely ignore ViewResolver.

question: What is HttpMessageConverter in Spring MVC?
title: HttpMessageConverter in Spring — Serialization and Deserialization
direct_answer: HttpMessageConverter converts Java objects to HTTP response bodies (serialization) and HTTP request bodies to Java objects (deserialization). MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter handles JSON. Spring Boot auto-configures it when Jackson is on the classpath.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how @RequestBody and @ResponseBody actually work under the hood
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Jackson just works magically without understanding the MessageConverter chain and content negotiation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain content negotiation — Spring selects the converter based on Accept and Content-Type headers, trying each registered converter in order

sections.title: The Serialization Bridge Between Java and HTTP
sections.content: **HttpMessageConverter** is the Spring MVC component that handles **serialization** (converting Java objects to HTTP response bodies) and **deserialization** (converting HTTP request bodies to Java objects). When you annotate a controller method with **@ResponseBody** or use **@RestController**, Spring uses an HttpMessageConverter to convert your return value into the response format — typically JSON. When you use **@RequestBody**, Spring uses a converter to parse the incoming request body into a Java object. The most common converter is **MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter**, which handles JSON using the Jackson library. Spring maintains a list of registered converters and selects one based on **content negotiation** — it checks the `Accept` header (for responses) and `Content-Type` header (for requests) to decide which converter to use. Spring Boot auto-configures Jackson's converter when it detects Jackson on the classpath, which happens by default with spring-boot-starter-web. You can register custom converters for XML, Protobuf, or proprietary formats by implementing HttpMessageConverter and adding it to the WebMvcConfigurer.

sections.title: HttpMessageConverter in Action with REST Controller
Key Points
content: **Serialization**: HttpMessageConverter converts Java objects to HTTP response bodies — e.g., Customer object to JSON string
**Deserialization**: Converts HTTP request bodies to Java objects — e.g., JSON string to Customer object via @RequestBody
**MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter**: Default converter for JSON — auto-configured by Spring Boot when Jackson is on classpath
**Content Negotiation**: Spring selects a converter based on Accept header (responses) and Content-Type header (requests)
**Converter Chain**: Spring tries each registered HttpMessageConverter in order until one can handle the content type
**@ResponseBody**: Signals Spring to use HttpMessageConverter instead of ViewResolver — implicit in @RestController
**Custom Converters**: Implement HttpMessageConverter and register via WebMvcConfigurer to support XML, Protobuf, or custom formats

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: HttpMessageConverter is the component that translates between Java objects and HTTP message bodies. When you return a Java object from a REST controller, Spring needs to convert it to JSON or XML to send over the wire. That's serialization. When a client sends JSON in the request body and you use at-RequestBody, Spring needs to parse that JSON into a Java object. That's deserialization. HttpMessageConverter does both jobs. The most common one is MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, which handles JSON using the Jackson library. Spring Boot auto-configures it when Jackson is on the classpath, which it is by default in spring-boot-starter-web. Spring maintains a list of registered converters. When a request comes in, it picks the right converter using content negotiation. For incoming requests, it checks the Content-Type header. If the header says application/json, Spring uses the Jackson converter. For outgoing responses, it checks the Accept header. If the client sent Accept: application/json, Spring uses Jackson to serialize your return value. One thing freshers don't realize is the converter chain. Spring tries each registered converter in order until one says, "I can handle this." That's why you can have multiple converters for different formats like JSON, XML, and plain text. If you need to support a custom format, you implement HttpMessageConverter and register it by overriding configureMessageConverters in WebMvcConfigurer.

speakable_v2.hook: When you return a Java object from a @RestController, something has to turn it into JSON bytes. That something is HttpMessageConverter.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: HttpMessageConverter handles both directions: it reads incoming request bodies and writes outgoing response bodies. For JSON, the default converter is MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, auto-configured when Jackson is on the classpath.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Spring selects the right converter using content negotiation. For writing a response, it checks the Accept header the client sent. For reading a request body, it checks the Content-Type header. If you send JSON with Content-Type application/json, Spring uses Jackson to deserialize it into your @RequestBody parameter.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter: handles JSON. Auto-configured. Used for most REST APIs.
StringHttpMessageConverter: for String return types, produces text/plain.
ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter: for binary data like file downloads.
Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter: handles XML if jackson-dataformat-xml is on the classpath.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: gotcha: If a client sends Accept: application/xml but you only have the JSON converter configured, Spring returns 406 Not Acceptable — not a serialization error. The converter chain is checked before your method return value is touched.

speakable_v2.cap: Customize Jackson by defining an ObjectMapper bean — Spring Boot will use yours instead of the default configuration.
